title: Climate-driven chemistry and aerosol feedbacks in CMIP6 Earth system models
abstract: Abstract. Feedbacks play a fundamental role in determining the magnitude of the response of the climate system to external forcing, such as from anthropogenic emissions. The latest generation of Earth system models includes aerosol and chemistry components that interact with each other and with the biosphere. These interactions introduce a complex web of feedbacks that is important to understand and quantify. This paper addresses multiple pathways for aerosol and chemical feedbacks in Earth system models. These focus on changes in natural emissions (dust, sea salt, dimethyl sulfide, biogenic volatile organic compounds (BVOCs) and lightning) and changes in reaction rates for methane and ozone chemistry. The feedback terms are then given by the sensitivity of a pathway to climate change multiplied by the radiative effect of the change. We find that the overall climate feedback through chemistry and aerosols is negative in the sixth Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6) Earth system models due to increased negative forcing from aerosols in a climate with warmer surface temperatures following a quadrupling of CO2 concentrations. This is principally due to increased emissions of sea salt and BVOCs which are sensitive to climate change and cause strong negative radiative forcings. Increased chemical loss of ozone and methane also contributes to a negative feedback. However, overall methane lifetime is expected to increase in a warmer climate due to increased BVOCs. Increased emissions of methane from wetlands would also offset some of the negative feedbacks. The CMIP6 experimental design did not allow the methane lifetime or methane emission changes to affect climate, so we found a robust negative contribution from interactive aerosols and chemistry to climate sensitivity in CMIP6 Earth system models.
field: Aerosol and atmospheric chemistry climate feedbacks
problem: While Earth system models include interactive aerosol and chemistry components, the complex web of resulting feedbacks is poorly understood and quantified, creating uncertainty about their effect on the climate system's response to external forcing.
method: This paper quantifies aerosol and chemical feedbacks by diagnosing the sensitivity of natural emissions to climate and their radiative efficiencies, using results from a suite of idealized Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 6 (CMIP6) Earth system model experiments.
task: The task is to quantify multiple pathways for climate-driven aerosol and chemical feedbacks in CMIP6 Earth system models by analyzing changes in natural emissions and reaction rates for methane and ozone chemistry under a warming scenario.
innovation: This paper quantifies multiple aerosol and chemical feedbacks in CMIP6 Earth system models, finding that the overall feedback is negative, dampening climate warming primarily due to increased emissions of sea salt and biogenic volatile organic compounds in a warmer climate.

The level of sophistication of the chemistry can affect the modelled responses to the emissions of reactive gases. For instance, in models without interactive tropospheric chemistry, changes in BVOCs affect only organic aerosols, whereas in models with interactive tropospheric chemistry, they also affect ozone, methane lifetime and potentially the oxidation of other aerosol precursors.

The ESMs used in CMIP6 all use a cloud-top-height parameterisation of lightning. Such schemes have previously been found to increase lightning production in warmer climates, whereas more sophisticated schemes based on convective updraft mass flux or ice flux show decreases in lightning with temperature (Clark et al., 2017; Finney et al., 2016b, 2018). The result from the Atmospheric Chemistry and Climate Model Intercomparison (ACCMIP) of 0.44 Tg(N) yr−1 K−1 (Finney et al., 2016a) lies within the range of the models with increased lightning under 4xCO2 (0.27 to 0.61 Tg(N) yr−1 K−1).
